title: Objects, ownership and controllers
summary: ownerReferences, garbage collection, finalizers, how a rollout really works, and what an operator is.

concepts.title: ownerReferences and garbage collection
concepts.brief:
Kubernetes has no foreign keys. Instead, a child object carries `metadata.ownerReferences` pointing at its parent, and the **garbage collector** deletes children whose owner is gone.

`Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod` is two owner links, not one object doing three jobs.

Deletion has three propagation policies:

- **Background** (default for kubectl): the owner is deleted immediately, children are cleaned up afterwards
- **Foreground**: the owner sits in `deletionTimestamp` with a `foregroundDeletion` finalizer until every child is gone, then it disappears
- **Orphan**: children are kept and their ownerReference is stripped

Owner and child must be in the same namespace (or the owner cluster-scoped). A cross-namespace ownerReference is invalid and gets the child deleted — a real trap when generating manifests.

examples.label: The chain, visible
examples.code:
$ kubectl get rs -l app=api
NAME              DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
api-6b8f9c7d4d    3         3         3       5d

$ kubectl get rs api-6b8f9c7d4d -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences}' | jq
[{"apiVersion":"apps/v1","kind":"Deployment","name":"api",
  "uid":"3f2b...","controller":true,"blockOwnerDeletion":true}]
examples.note: `uid`, not name. Delete and recreate a Deployment with the same name and the old ReplicaSets are orphaned — the uid no longer matches.

examples.label: Keeping the pods when deleting the parent
examples.code:
$ kubectl delete deployment api --cascade=orphan
deployment.apps "api" deleted

$ kubectl get pods -l app=api
NAME                    READY   STATUS    AGE
api-6b8f9c7d4d-xk2p9    1/1     Running   5d      # still there, now unmanaged
examples.note: Useful in migrations when you want to replace a controller without restarting the workload.

items.prompt: Order the ownership chain from a `kubectl create deployment` to a running container.
steps: Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet owned by the Deployment
ReplicaSet controller creates Pods owned by the ReplicaSet
Scheduler binds each pod to a node
That node's kubelet starts the containers
items.explain: Five independent actors, each watching for its own input. Nobody orchestrates the sequence — it emerges from each controller doing its narrow job.

items.prompt: You delete Deployment `api` and immediately recreate it with the same name and spec. What happens to the old ReplicaSets?
choices: They are garbage collected — ownerReferences match on UID, and the new Deployment has a new UID
They are adopted by the new Deployment because the name matches
They stay forever as orphans
They are adopted only if the pod-template hash matches
items.explain: Ownership is by UID. The old RS points at a UID that no longer exists, so the GC removes it (and its pods). Same reason: never reuse a name and expect continuity — and never hand-write an ownerReference without the right UID.

items.prompt: Match the deletion policy to its behaviour.
pairs: Owner deleted at once, children cleaned up after
Owner stays Terminating until all children are gone
Children survive with their ownerReference removed
items.explain: `kubectl delete --cascade=background|foreground|orphan`. Foreground is what you want when a controller must not see a half-deleted tree; orphan is the migration escape hatch.

items.prompt: A generated manifest gives a ConfigMap in namespace `app` an ownerReference to a Deployment in namespace `platform`. What happens?
choices: The reference is invalid; the garbage collector treats the owner as missing and deletes the ConfigMap
It works — ownerReferences are cluster-scoped
The API server rejects the ConfigMap at admission
The ConfigMap is silently moved to the platform namespace
items.explain: Cross-namespace ownership is not supported. The GC looks for the owner *in the child's namespace*, does not find it, and cleans up. Objects mysteriously vanishing minutes after creation is the classic symptom.

concepts.title: Finalizers and stuck deletions
concepts.brief:
A finalizer is a string in `metadata.finalizers` that means: *do not actually delete this object until I have cleaned up*.

Deleting an object with finalizers does not remove it. The API server sets `metadata.deletionTimestamp` and the object stays visible, `Terminating`, until every finalizer is removed by whoever owns it.

This is how a controller detaches a cloud load balancer before its Service disappears, or wipes a bucket before its CR goes.

When the controller that owns a finalizer is uninstalled, nothing removes it — and the object hangs forever. A namespace stuck `Terminating` is nearly always one leftover object with an unsatisfied finalizer, most often a CR whose operator is gone.

examples.label: Finding what is actually blocking a namespace
examples.code:
$ kubectl get ns prod -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' | jq -r '.[].message'
Some resources are remaining: databases.acid.zalan.do has 1 resource instances

# find the object and its finalizer
$ kubectl get databases.acid.zalan.do -n prod -o json |
    jq '.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, fin:.metadata.finalizers}'
{ "name": "orders-db", "fin": ["postgres-operator.acid.zalan.do/finalizer"] }
examples.note: Read the namespace *conditions* first. Force-deleting the namespace object hides the problem and leaks the underlying resources.

examples.label: Removing a finalizer, deliberately
examples.code:
# only after confirming the external resource is really gone
$ kubectl patch database orders-db -n prod --type=json \
    -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/metadata/finalizers"}]'
database.acid.zalan.do/orders-db patched
examples.note: This is deleting the safety catch, not fixing the cause. Whatever the operator was going to clean up (a volume, a DNS record, a cloud LB) is now your problem.

items.prompt: What does `kubectl delete` do to an object that has a finalizer?
choices: Sets deletionTimestamp and leaves the object in place until the finalizer is removed
Deletes it and lets the controller clean up asynchronously
Fails with a 409 Conflict
Removes the finalizer automatically after 30 seconds
items.explain: The object becomes read-mostly and `Terminating`. Nothing times it out. Understanding this turns 'the namespace won't delete' from a mystery into a two-command diagnosis.

items.prompt: Namespace `prod` has been `Terminating` for two hours. What is the right first command?
choices: kubectl get ns prod -o json | jq .status.conditions — to see which resources remain
Patch the namespace to drop its own finalizer
Restart kube-controller-manager
Delete the namespace with --force --grace-period=0
items.explain: The namespace status names the API group that still has instances. Removing the *namespace's* `kubernetes` finalizer forces the object out of etcd while leaving orphaned resources behind — sometimes still billing you in a cloud account.

items.prompt: You force-remove a finalizer from a CR whose operator was uninstalled. What might be left behind?
choices: A cloud load balancer that nothing will delete
A persistent volume in the storage backend
A DNS record or firewall rule created by the operator
Corruption of the etcd database
items.explain: The finalizer existed because something outside Kubernetes needed cleanup. etcd itself is fine — but your cloud bill may not be. Reinstall the operator, let it clean up properly, then uninstall it.

items.prompt: Which field does the API server set instead of deleting an object that has finalizers?
items.explain: `metadata.deletionTimestamp`. Controllers watch for it as the signal to start cleanup, then remove their finalizer. When the list is empty, the object is really deleted.

concepts.title: How a rollout actually works
concepts.brief:
A Deployment never updates a Pod. It creates a **new ReplicaSet** and shifts replicas from old to new.

The new RS is named with a hash of the pod template, and that hash is also a label on the pods. Change the template → new hash → new RS. Change something outside the template (like `replicas`) → same RS, just resized.

Two knobs control the shape of the transition:

- `maxSurge` — how many pods *above* the desired count may exist during the roll
- `maxUnavailable` — how many below `replicas` may be unready

With `maxUnavailable: 0` you always keep full capacity but need room for surge pods. With `maxSurge: 0` you never exceed the replica count but dip in capacity.

Progress is judged by `progressDeadlineSeconds` (default 600). When it expires the Deployment gets `Progressing=False` with reason `ProgressDeadlineExceeded` — it does **not** roll back on its own.

examples.label: Two ReplicaSets during a roll
examples.code:
$ kubectl get rs -l app=api
NAME              DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
api-6b8f9c7d4d    1         1         1       5d     # old, draining
api-7d4c5b8a91    3         3         2       25s    # new, filling

$ kubectl rollout status deploy/api
Waiting for deployment "api" rollout to finish: 2 of 3 updated replicas are available...
examples.note: The old RS is kept at 0 replicas afterwards (see `revisionHistoryLimit`) — that is what `kubectl rollout undo` scales back up.

examples.label: Surge and unavailability
examples.code:
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1            # at most 5 pods exist at once
      maxUnavailable: 0      # never fewer than 4 ready
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
examples.note: maxUnavailable: 0 needs spare cluster capacity for the surge pod, otherwise the roll simply stalls with a Pending pod.

examples.label: A stalled rollout speaks
examples.code:
$ kubectl describe deploy api | grep -A4 Conditions
Conditions:
  Type           Status  Reason
  Available      True    MinimumReplicasAvailable
  Progressing    False   ProgressDeadlineExceeded

$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/api            # back to the previous RS
$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/api --to-revision=3

items.prompt: You change the image in a Deployment. What does the Deployment controller do?
choices: Creates a new ReplicaSet with a new pod-template hash and shifts replicas from the old one to it
Updates each existing pod's image in place
Deletes all pods, then recreates them with the new image
Tells the kubelets to pull the new image and restart the containers
items.explain: Pods are immutable in the ways that matter — the container image of a running pod is not edited in place. The unit of change is the ReplicaSet, which is exactly why rollback is just scaling the old RS back up.

items.prompt: `replicas: 10`, `maxSurge: 25%`, `maxUnavailable: 25%`. During the roll, what is the max total pods and min available?
choices: Max 13 pods total, min 8 available
Max 10 pods total, min 8 available
Max 13 pods total, min 10 available
Max 12 pods total, min 7 available
items.explain: Percentages are of `replicas`: surge rounds up (10 + ceil(2.5) = 13), unavailable rounds down (10 - floor(2.5) = 8). Getting this wrong is how a rolling update quietly halves your capacity at peak.

items.prompt: A rollout is stuck: `Progressing=False, reason=ProgressDeadlineExceeded`. What did Kubernetes do about it?
choices: Nothing — it recorded the condition and left both ReplicaSets in place; rollback is a manual decision
It automatically rolled back to the previous revision
It deleted the new ReplicaSet
It restarted the deployment controller
items.explain: There is no auto-rollback in core Kubernetes. The condition is a signal for your CD tooling (Argo Rollouts, Flux) or a human. `kubectl rollout undo` is the manual fix.

items.prompt: Which `kubectl` command restarts every pod of a Deployment without changing its image?
items.explain: `kubectl rollout restart deploy/api` adds a `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` annotation to the **pod template**. That changes the template hash, so a new ReplicaSet is created and the normal rolling update carries it out — respecting maxSurge/maxUnavailable and your PDBs.

concepts.title: CRDs and operators
concepts.brief:
A **CustomResourceDefinition** extends the API server with a new resource type. Once registered, your CR gets the whole machinery for free: RBAC, `kubectl get`, watches, admission, audit logs, etcd storage.

A CRD alone does nothing but store objects. An **operator** is the controller that gives it meaning — the same watch/reconcile loop as any built-in controller, just running in a pod.

Things worth knowing operationally:

- CRDs are **cluster-scoped** objects, even when the resources they define are namespaced
- Deleting a CRD deletes **every CR of that type** across all namespaces — a genuinely destructive act
- Multiple versions can be served with a **conversion webhook**; exactly one is the storage version
- A `status` subresource lets the controller write status without touching spec (and vice versa)

Rancher, cert-manager, Fleet and the RKE2 helm-controller are all this pattern.

examples.label: A CRD and its instance
examples.code:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: backups.ops.example.com     # must be <plural>.<group>
spec:
  group: ops.example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names: { plural: backups, singular: backup, kind: Backup, shortNames: [bk] }
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true                    # exactly one version is the storage version
    subresources: { status: {} }
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            required: [schedule]
            properties:
              schedule: { type: string }

examples.label: The blast radius of deleting a CRD
examples.code:
$ kubectl get backups -A --no-headers | wc -l
214

$ kubectl delete crd backups.ops.example.com
# all 214 Backup objects are deleted, in every namespace
examples.note: Helm uninstall does not usually remove CRDs, precisely because of this. Removing one by hand during a 'cleanup' has ended more than one production evening.

examples.label: The RKE2 helm-controller does exactly this
examples.code:
$ kubectl -n kube-system get helmcharts.helm.cattle.io
NAME                    JOB                          CHART
rke2-canal              helm-install-rke2-canal      rke2-canal
rke2-coredns            helm-install-rke2-coredns    rke2-coredns
rke2-ingress-nginx      helm-install-rke2-ingress..  rke2-ingress-nginx
examples.note: A HelmChart CR is reconciled by spawning a Job that runs helm. That is how RKE2 installs its own add-ons using nothing but the Kubernetes API.

items.prompt: You apply a CRD and create three custom resources. No operator is installed. What happens?
choices: The objects are stored and queryable, but nothing acts on them
The API server rejects them without a controller registered
kube-controller-manager reconciles them generically
They stay Pending until an operator claims them
items.explain: A CRD is a schema plus storage. Meaning comes from a controller. This is also why a stuck CR with a finalizer never resolves once its operator is uninstalled — nobody is left to remove the finalizer.

items.prompt: What is the effect of `kubectl delete crd certificates.cert-manager.io` on a cluster using cert-manager?
choices: Every Certificate object in every namespace is deleted along with the type
Only the CRD is removed; existing Certificates remain until recreated
The command is rejected while instances exist
Certificates become read-only
items.explain: Deleting a CRD cascades to all its instances cluster-wide. Combined with finalizers, the deletion can also hang halfway. Treat CRD deletion with the same care as dropping a database table.

items.prompt: Which statement about CRD scoping is right?
choices: The CRD object itself is cluster-scoped; the resources it defines can be Namespaced or Cluster
Both the CRD and its resources are always namespaced
A namespaced CRD only serves its own namespace
Scope is chosen per custom resource at creation time
items.explain: `spec.scope: Namespaced|Cluster` controls the instances. The definition always lives cluster-wide — which is why two teams cannot install conflicting versions of the same CRD in different namespaces.

items.prompt: Why enable the `status` subresource on a CRD?
choices: So the controller can update status without touching spec, and users updating spec cannot clobber status
So status appears in kubectl get output
It is required for the CRD to be served
It enables server-side apply
items.explain: It splits the object into two endpoints with separate write paths and RBAC. Without it, every status write is a full object update racing with user edits — a reliable source of 409 storms in a busy operator.
